decisions.notebook: Game 3 lost: Corviknight+Snorlax vs Milotic+Sinistcha. Key lessons: (1) Sinistcha Protect streak made it predictable but Corviknight couldn't break through—Brave Bird kept getting blocked. Should have targeted Milotic with U-turn chip earlier or used Snorlax EQ more aggressively when Sinistcha was likely to Protect. (2) Milotic Competitive +4 SpA is devastating—avoid Icy Wind triggers on Milotic at all costs. Mirror Armor bouncing Intimidate was useful but Icy Wind self-triggered Competitive twice. (3) Snorlax accuracy -1 from Muddy Water made Fire Punch (56%) and Body Slam (64%) unreliable; EQ was the only safe option but too weak vs Grass-type Sinistcha. (4) Strength Sap on physical attackers is game-ending—need to KO Sinistcha before it can use it, or bring a special attacker. Series tied 1-1 heading into potential game 3 conclusion.

reflections.summary: Won Game 3 and the series 2-1 through a strong Milotic/Sinistcha endgame: Competitive turned Corviknight’s Mirror Armor-reflected Icy Wind drops into major Special Attack boosts, while Sinistcha safely stalled and redirected pressure. Gholdengo also removed Mega Metagross and Skeledirge, though its entry was costly and it was ultimately exposed to Snorlax’s Fire Punch. The four brought were broadly suitable, but Arcanine was a poor fit for the demonstrated Metagross/Corviknight pressure and contributed little before being KOed. No own Mega Stone holder was available or evolved, so there is no evidence that a different Mega choice was missed. The zero-error game indicates clean piloting; the supplied evidence does not include Games 1-2 or explicit between-game plans, so whether the adjustment from earlier games helped or backfired cannot be established. The registered six and their shown sets got the important parts right—Competitive Milotic, defensive Sinistcha, and offensive Gholdengo—but there is insufficient evidence to say that Tauros, Lopunny, Furfrou, or Chimecho would have been better choices.
reflections.adjustment: Against a rematch, preserve the Milotic/Sinistcha core and use Icy Wind deliberately into Mirror Armor targets, accepting the reflected drop for Competitive boosts. Give Gholdengo a safer entry and avoid leaving it exposed to Ground or Fire coverage. Reconsider Arcanine as the fourth slot, especially if its Intimidate is likely to be reflected or if Metagross can immediately target it with Earthquake; consider one of the registered alternatives only if its actual set supplies reliable speed control, disruption, or protection. Do not assume an unevolved team is inferior without a demonstrated Mega option. The available evidence cannot validate a specific between-game adjustment or prove that any left-behind Pokémon would have outperformed Arcanine.
reflections.notebook: Milotic Competitive is a major weapon against Intimidate and Mirror Armor: reflected Icy Wind drops can produce large Special Attack boosts, so preserve Milotic when practical. Corviknight revealed Mirror Armor, Tailwind, U-turn, Brave Bird, and Protect; avoid treating speed drops as ordinary and expect it to pressure Sinistcha physically. Mega Metagross was Jolly with Protect, Earthquake, Meteor Mash, and Bullet Punch; Earthquake threatens both exposed Fire- and Steel-types and can punish careless Gholdengo positioning. Snorlax was Adamant with Thick Fat, Leftovers, Protect, Body Slam, Earthquake, and Fire Punch; it can absorb Fire pressure, ignore speed-control attempts only imperfectly, and punish Gholdengo with Fire Punch. Skeledirge revealed Unaware, Torch Song, Shadow Ball, Will-O-Wisp, and Protect, so do not rely on accumulated boosts alone against it. Sinistcha remains valuable for Rage Powder, Strength Sap, Protect, and Ground immunity, but avoid Crunch, Taunt, and concentrated physical pressure. Preparation should prioritize a safe Gholdengo entry, dependable answers to Mega Metagross plus Snorlax, and a fourth slot more resilient than Arcanine if these same threats return. The available games do not establish reliable broader opponent tendencies beyond these revealed sets and choices.

reflections.summary: The game and series were lost at team preview and compounded by a fatal mechanic interaction. Corviknight's Mirror Armor bounced Icy Wind's Speed drop onto Milotic, triggering Competitive for +2 SpA each time (turns 1 and 6, totaling +4). This turned Milotic into an unstoppable special sweeper that chunked Metagross to 33% by turn 2 and invalidated Snorlax's accuracy with Muddy Water. Bringing Corviknight against a Competitive Milotic was actively self-destructive. Mega Metagross died to Gholdengo Shadow Ball before dealing meaningful damage beyond the Arcanine KO. Skeledirge (Unaware, the natural Milotic answer) was brought but never acted—died to Gholdengo Shadow Ball on turn 5 before moving. Toxapex, registered but left on the bench, had Haze to reset Milotic's boosts and a Water resistance; its omission was the decisive prep error. By the time it was Snorlax alone versus Milotic at +4 and a full-health Sinistcha with Strength Sap, the position was unwinnable.
reflections.adjustment: Never bring Corviknight against this opponent's Competitive Milotic—the Mirror Armor/Icy Wind interaction is a trap that gifts +2 SpA per hit. In a future series, bring Toxapex (Haze + Recover) as the primary Milotic answer and pair it with a special attacker that can pressure Sinistcha (Greninja, left behind this series, would qualify). If Mega Metagross is brought, protect it from Gholdengo Shadow Ball better—consider leading it away from Gholdengo or bringing a switch-in that absorbs Ghost. Skeledirge's Unaware is valuable against Competitive but it is too slow to survive Gholdengo; either bring a Gholdengo answer alongside it or don't bring it at all. Reconsider whether Mega Metagross is the right Mega here versus a team with Gholdengo; an alternative Mega or no-Mega build with better defensive synergy may serve better.
reflections.notebook: Opponent tendencies: brings Milotic (Competitive, Icy Wind/Muddy Water/Recover/Protect, Modest, Leftovers) + Sinistcha (Rage Powder/Matcha Gotcha/Strength Sap/Protect, Hospitality, Calm, Sitrus) as a core; supports with Arcanine (Intimidate, Heat Wave/Snarl/WoW/Protect) and Gholdengo (Make It Rain/Shadow Ball/Focus Blast/Protect, Good as Gold, Life Orb, Modest). Whimsicott (Prankster Tailwind/Encore/Taunt/Moonblast, Focus Sash) and Grimmsnarl (Prankster screens/Parting Shot/Spirit Break, Light Clay) available but not brought in game 3. Strategic facts: (1) Mirror Armor Corviknight triggers Competitive Milotic via Icy Wind bounce—avoid this pairing entirely. (2) Milotic uses Icy Wind specifically to self-trigger Competitive; any Speed-lowering effect bounced onto it is catastrophic. (3) Sinistcha Protect-streaks under pressure and uses Strength Sap to invalidate physical attackers; special attackers are required to break it. (4) Gholdengo outspeeds and OHKOs Skeledirge with Shadow Ball; do not leave Skeledirge exposed to it. (5) Opponent protects Sinistcha with Rage Powder to redirect attacks away from Milotic. Prep conclusions: Toxapex (Haze) is mandatory against this opponent. A fast special attacker (Greninja) is needed for Sinistcha. Corviknight is a liability here. Snorlax is decent as a Gholdengo answer with Earthquake but struggles once accuracy drops. Mega Metagross is fragile against Gholdengo and Muddy Water chip; weigh whether its offensive output justifies the slot.
